clue.text: Face up to Tony in desperation keeping money — I don't like it

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it within, so the phrase before it holds the next item inside
desperation suggests frantic disorder, so the letters are thrown into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
M is the standard abbreviation for money

explanation.surface: Someone in a desperate state has to confront a man called Tony while holding on to cash, and hates the whole business.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something is not your cup of tea is an idiom meaning you dislike or have no taste for it.

clue.text: Rarely used loos round side though seemingly hygienic

indicators.note: going round something encloses it
done rarely means done in an unusual way, so the letters take an odd new order

parts.note: taken as written
R for right, one side

explanation.surface: Toilets that hardly anyone uses, around one side of a building, appear to be clean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rarely used' reads as one phrase, but 'Rarely' is the shuffle signal acting on the next two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Having no smell suggests cleanliness, though it is only a sign of hygiene, hence the hedge in the clue.

clue.text: Joins baseball team touring East

indicators.note: a team touring a place goes all around it, so it encloses the next item

parts.note: the New York Mets
standard abbreviation of East

explanation.surface: A baseball side links up with others on a trip through the eastern states.
explanation.definitionFit: Where two roads meet they join, so meets is a synonym for connects or unites with.

clue.text: Tradesman's shop

definitions.meaning: first meaning: British slang for a carpenter
second meaning: British slang for a fish and chip shop

explanation.walkthrough: The 's looks possessive, making a tradesman's workshop; it is 'is', joining two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a carpenter or joiner is nicknamed a chippie, and so is a takeaway selling fish and chips.

clue.text: Seed having nightmare on green, Spooner reported

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so we say the phrase his way

parts.note: needing nine putts would be a golfer's nightmare on the green

explanation.surface: A golfer's grass seed has had a dreadful time on the putting green.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening sounds of the golfing disaster and you get the edible seed.
explanation.definitionFit: Pine nuts are the edible seeds of certain pine trees, used in pesto.

clue.text: Sick of glamour oddly peculiar to some of Dylan's work

indicators.note: something peculiar is strange and out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: oddly here means the odd letters are discarded, keeping every other one

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Bob Dylan's songs as a reaction against showbiz glitz, which his early work arguably was.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' here keeps the even letters, dropping the odd ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Bob Dylan began his career in the folk revival, so part of his output is traditional-style acoustic song.

clue.text: Before being put outside, turned up in drawer initially

indicators.note: in a down answer, turned up means read from bottom to top
putting one thing outside another wraps it around that other

parts.note: ere is an old word for before
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something was flipped up inside a drawer before being taken outside.
explanation.walkthrough: ERNIE is the machine that draws Premium Bond prize numbers in Britain; its name is an acronym, hence 'initially'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Premium Bonds winners are drawn by a machine named from the initials Electronic Random Number Indicator Equipment.

clue.text: Less people from school joining force — they won't like it

parts.note: a grammar school, a selective British secondary school
the police force

explanation.surface: Fewer pupils leave school to join the police, and the officers are unhappy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Less people' is the kind of slip that pedants correct to 'fewer people', so it sets up the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Pedants who correct others' usage are mockingly called the grammar police, and 'less people' is a usage they object to.

clue.text: Hated escorting right away: unfortunate but don't give up too soon!

indicators.note: unfortunate suggests things have gone awry, so the letters fall into a new order
something sent away is gone, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
the usual abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Being a hated escort is miserable, but someone urges the sufferer to stick it out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'escorting' looks like a container signal, but it is fodder that loses its R before the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: To go the distance is an idiom from boxing for lasting to the end rather than quitting early.

clue.text: Old African's letter to boys

parts.note: a Greek letter
two boys' names, Des and Ian

explanation.surface: An elderly man from Africa writes a letter to some lads.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is': the old African is the letter followed by two boys' names.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhodesia was the former name of Zimbabwe, so a citizen of that vanished state is an African of former times.

clue.text: In retrospect, a mistake defending FA's language

indicators.note: retrospect means looking backwards, so the pieces are read from end to start

parts.note: an own goal, the classic defender's error in football, abbreviated OG
FA as in 'sweet FA', slang for nothing at all

explanation.surface: Looking back, a football error cost the Football Association its tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: FA looks like the Football Association, chiming with the own goal, but 'sweet FA' is British slang for nothing; the 's is 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lingo is an informal word for a language or jargon, especially a foreign or unfamiliar one.

clue.text: Former Chancellor's usual way of doing things

parts.note: Sir Thomas More, Lord Chancellor under Henry VIII
the possessive ending taken as the letter

explanation.surface: A description of how some ex-Chancellor of the Exchequer habitually went about things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Former Chancellor' points to recent Treasury ministers, but the man is Thomas More, Henry VIII's Lord Chancellor.
explanation.definitionFit: Mores are the customs and conventions of a community, its accepted habits of behaviour.

clue.text: 'Quiet!' Hard to handle French nurse in pub in capital

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another places it within that other item

parts.note: p, piano, is the musical mark for quiet
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard
a handle is a name, which in French is nom
PH, public house, as on Ordnance Survey maps
an EN is an enrolled nurse

explanation.surface: Someone in a bar is told to hush because a French nurse there is tricky to manage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Handle' is slang for a name, and French puts it as NOM; the nurse sits inside the pub at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Phnom Penh is the capital city of Cambodia, on the Mekong river.

clue.text: Mean to declare how long you've been here

parts.note: to aver is to state firmly
your age measures your time alive

explanation.surface: Someone intends to announce how long they have lived or stayed somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean to' reads as 'intend to', but 'Mean' stands alone as the noun from statistics.
explanation.definitionFit: In arithmetic the mean and the average are the same figure: the total divided by the count.

clue.text: 'O Claudius' is wrong? That's harsh

indicators.note: something wrong is out of order, so these letters must be put right in a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A critic condemns a line addressing Claudius, as in Hamlet, as mistaken and cruel.
explanation.definitionFit: Acidulous means sharp or sour, and so is used of biting, cutting remarks.

clue.text: Bottom of river is experimental site

parts.note: the Test is a chalk-stream river in Hampshire, England
a river's bottom is its bed

explanation.surface: The floor of some river is being used as a place for scientific trials.
explanation.walkthrough: The river is named first and its bottom follows, so the clue's order is turned round in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A test bed is a place or piece of equipment where new devices or ideas are tried out.

clue.text: Woodland residents keeping alert in Chelsea?

indicators.note: keeping something means holding it inside

parts.note: the nickname of Chelsea Football Club, a London team
an alarm bell gives an alert

explanation.surface: Forest dwellers staying watchful in a smart London district.
explanation.walkthrough: Chelsea is both a London district and a football club whose nickname is the Blues.
explanation.definitionFit: Bluebells carpet British woods in spring, so they are playfully called residents of the woodland.

clue.text: I don't know Vlad's voice

parts.note: what a quiz contestant says when stumped
Vlad is the setter, so 'Vlad has' becomes 'I have', contracted

explanation.surface: The setter admits he cannot say what his own speaking voice is like.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters refer to themselves by pseudonym; 'Vlad's' means 'Vlad has', which from his mouth is I'VE.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar the passive is one of the voices of a verb, alongside the active.

clue.text: Stone me! Romeo in wood ignoring women

indicators.note: what goes in something is placed inside it
ignoring something leaves it out

parts.note: a weald is old word for woodland, as in the Weald of Kent
W is the abbreviation for women
Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet
taken as written

explanation.surface: An exclamation of surprise about Romeo hiding in a forest without any women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stone me!' reads as an old British exclamation of surprise, but 'Stone' alone defines.
explanation.definitionFit: An emerald is a green gemstone, a precious variety of beryl.

clue.text: You shouldn't slip on these

parts.note: surface reading: a warning about a slippery floor or icy steps
setter's reading: these shoes are not the slip-on kind, as they must be tied

explanation.walkthrough: 'Slip on' suggests falling over; read as putting shoes on without fastening, it points to the opposite kind of shoe.
explanation.definitionFit: Shoes fastened with laces cannot simply be slipped onto the feet, unlike loafers or slip-ons.

clue.text: Give up on sad song

parts.note: a lay is a ballad or song
feeling down is feeling sad

explanation.surface: Someone abandons a melancholy ballad.
explanation.walkthrough: The parts appear in reverse: the song comes first in the answer, then the sad part.
explanation.definitionFit: To lay down arms or one's office is to surrender or relinquish them.

clue.text: Relaxing wear for Hawaii? Of course

parts.note: a garland of flowers worn round the neck in Hawaii
both phrases agree emphatically

explanation.surface: Someone asks if casual clothes are what you wear in Hawaii, and gets a yes.
explanation.definitionFit: Something leisurely is unhurried and calm, done in a relaxed manner with no rush.

clue.text: Spiritual sustenance Duke's lacking

indicators.note: lacking something means being without it, so that letter is removed

parts.note: a dinner is a meal
D is the abbreviation for Duke

explanation.surface: A nobleman goes without the nourishment of the soul.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spiritual sustenance' reads as one phrase; split it, as the 's means 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: The inner life is the life of the mind and soul, so inner can mean spiritual or mental.

clue.text: Assuming one's a little backbone

indicators.note: to assume is to take on or take in, so one item is taken inside another
going back means reading the result from its end to its start

parts.note: taken as written
the Roman numeral for one
a bit is a little amount
one printed word doing two jobs: its first half is the reversal signal, its second half the definition

explanation.surface: Supposing someone is a bit spineless, or has a small spine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backbone' looks like one word for the definition, but 'back' reverses and 'bone' alone defines.
explanation.definitionFit: The tibia is the shinbone, the larger of the two bones of the lower leg.

clue.text: Cat round Egypt raised as sacred object

indicators.note: going round something encloses it

parts.note: a tom is a male cat

indicators.note: raised in a down answer means read upwards, from bottom to top

parts.note: ET is the international vehicle code for Egypt

explanation.surface: A cat worshipped in ancient Egypt, raised as a holy figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' seems to belong with the whole cat, but it turns only the country code.
explanation.definitionFit: A totem is an object or emblem revered by a group as having spiritual significance.

clue.text: Cheats to get flat

parts.note: to con someone is to cheat them
to do someone is also British slang for cheating them

explanation.surface: Swindlers lie their way into an apartment.
explanation.walkthrough: One plural word supplies two synonyms in a row: to con and to do someone both mean to swindle them.
explanation.definitionFit: A condo, short for condominium, is an American term for an apartment owned within a shared building.

clue.text: The Pope's a Pole — look back with upright catholic

parts.note: taken as written
a pole or upright stake is a post

indicators.note: back tells us the word just before it runs from its end to its start

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look
the letter I is a single upright stroke
C is a standard abbreviation for Catholic

explanation.surface: Recalling John Paul II, a Polish pope, viewed alongside an upstanding Catholic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' suggests the Polish John Paul II, but it is just a post; the Pope's authority is called apostolic as he succeeds Peter.
explanation.definitionFit: Apostolic describes the pope or the papacy, since the pope claims succession from the apostle Peter.

clue.text: Joke — of kind — sees Trump getting irritated?

indicators.note: something irritated is agitated and stirred up, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A wisecrack that sees Donald Trump bristling, the way the 'who's really in charge' jibes did.
explanation.walkthrough: The dashes make 'of kind' look like an aside; it supplies four letters to the shuffled words that follow.
explanation.definitionFit: Critics mocked Elon Musk's influence over Trump's administration by calling him the real president, a jibe that reportedly annoyed Trump.
